# Part X: Frontiers and Limits {#part-frontiers .unnumbered}

> "For a successful technology, reality must take precedence over public
> relations, for nature cannot be fooled."
>
> Richard P. Feynman, ["Personal Observations on Reliability of Shuttle"](https://www.nasa.gov/history/rogersrep/v2appf.htm)

Part IX ended with machines that fail at cluster scale. This part asks what the
compute those machines supply is converted into. Compute is an input and
capability is an output. At the frontier, among the most capable systems built
so far, constraints become visible in the conversion between them. Three
constraints sit in that conversion, and more hardware removes none of them: the
stock of learnable signal, the instruments (benchmarks and evaluations) that
report how far the frontier has moved, and the cost of turning a produced claim
into an accepted one.

This part ends the book's account of capability itself. The parts after it take
capability as given and ask what is done with it: first the markets that price
and distribute it, then the practice of operating it. Taken together, the three
limits show that a frontier system is now constrained as often by what can be
known as by what can be built.

@sec-learning-limits starts on the input side, where the stock of high-quality
human text is finite and every proposed replacement remains contested: synthetic
data, learning from checked experience, spending compute at inference rather
than training, and models that keep learning after deployment.
@sec-capability-horizon turns to measurement. It examines the task-completion
horizon, the task length (in human completion time) that a model completes on
its own at a stated success rate. It shows that this number depends on the
success threshold and the test protocol, and that benchmarks saturate faster
than replacements can be built. @sec-verification-frontier closes on
acceptance. Where claims are cheaper to produce than to check, proof,
replication, adversarial review, and the institutions that grant trust have to
be built and operated as infrastructure.

Of the three limits, only the first, the stock of learnable signal, is likely to
ease with more spending; the other two concern instruments and trust. A compute
shortage, the limit Part IX covered, shows up as a queue and a bill. A shortage
of instruments or of trust shows up as a claim nobody can check, which takes far
longer to notice and costs more to correct.
